content: In 2012, cancer was responsible for approximately 2 million deaths, accounting for an estimated 13% of all global deaths. The World Health Organization (WHO) predicts a 70% increase in the number of new cancer cases over the next two decades, highlighting the substantial and growing burden of cancer worldwide. Among men in 2012, the most common cancers were lung, prostate, colorectal, gastric, and liver carcinomas. For women, the most prevalent cancers were breast, colorectal, lung, cervical, and gastric carcinomas. It is estimated that hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human papillomavirus (HPV) are responsible for up to 20% of cancer deaths in lowand middle-income countries. Furthermore, more than 30% of cancer cases are considered preventable through measures such as effective screening, vaccination, and lifestyle modifications. Breast cancer is the most common type of cancer (excluding non-melanoma skin cancers), with an estimated 249,000 new cases in the United States in 2016. Lung cancer and prostate cancer follow as the next most common cancers. In the United States, a cancer is classified as common if its estimated annual incidence is 40,000 cases or more. In 2013, the most frequently diagnosed cancers in children aged 0 to 19 years were leukemia and central nervous system cancers, which were also the leading causes of cancer-related deaths in this age group. Cancer Prevention Effective cancer prevention strategies include screening, vaccination, and lifestyle modifications. Breast Cancer Screening Studies have shown that breast cancer screening is associated with a reduction in breast cancer mortality of approximately 20% among women of all age groups with average risk. However, there is some uncertainty regarding the quantitative outcomes of different screening strategies in the United States. Colon Cancer Screening Screening colonoscopy has been reported to reduce the risk of colorectal cancer incidence and mortality by 40% to 60%. Cervical Cancer Screening Regular cervical cancer screenings can prevent approximately 70% to 80% of cervical cancer deaths. Lung Cancer Screening The National Lung Screening Trial (NLST), a randomized controlled trial involving 50,000 participants, demonstrated a 20% relative reduction in lung cancer mortality through screening. Vaccination HPV Vaccine The development of the quadrivalent HPV (4vHPV) vaccine has significantly decreased the prevalence of HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18 infections, as well as associated conditions such as genital warts, lowand high-grade cytological abnormalities, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grades 2 and 3, and adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) among females in their teens and twenties. Hepatitis B Vaccine Strong evidence supports the prevention of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) through the hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccine. A cluster randomized controlled trial involving the immunization of 75,000 newborns with the HBV vaccine demonstrated a significant reduction in HCC incidence. These findings suggest that preventing HBV infection can substantially reduce the burden of HCC. Lifestyle Modifications Lifestyle changes, such as maintaining a healthy diet, regular physical activity, avoiding tobacco use, and limiting alcohol consumption, play a critical role in reducing cancer risk.
